## pleasantry {.center}

### How a toy R package got built, with AI tools

Amelia Miramonti, Lincoln AI meetup

```{r}
set.seed(7)
compliment()
```

::: {.notes}
pleasantry is a small R package that makes random compliments and farewells.
This talk is about how it was built: at a workshop with Positron Assistant, then afterwards with Claude Code.
Every example on these slides is live R output, run with a fixed seed when the deck was rendered, so the jokes are the package's own.
:::

## What pleasantry is {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(5)
compliment(shakespearean = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
compliment(weirdness = 1)
set.seed(3)
compliment(mood = "grumpy")
```

::: {.notes}
Four exported functions: `compliment()`, `farewell()`, and an "of the day" version of each.
`compliment()` has a mood (sincere, grumpy, cheerful, dramatic), a Shakespearean switch, and a `weirdness` dial from 0 to 1.
Grumpy compliments are backhanded on purpose.
At weirdness 1 you get moth councils and pigeon diplomacy.
:::

## Profanity, with a dial

```{r}
set.seed(4)
compliment(profanity = "tame")
set.seed(1)
compliment(profanity = "mild")
set.seed(7)
compliment(profanity = "weird")
```

Five levels: `"none"`, `"tame"`, `"mild"`, `"strong"`, `"weird"`.
`"strong"` waits in the appendix, behind a warning.

::: {.notes}
`profanity` has five levels.
"tame" is the fudge-muffins level, "weird" swaps swearing for raccoon oracles.
The five-level argument is itself a result of the development story: it started as two arguments that said the same thing, and was merged into one.
The strong level is real four-letter words; it is in the appendix after a content warning, not in the main talk.
:::

## Stage 1: the workshop {.smaller}

- posit::conf(2026), Modern R workflow workshop, Monday 14 September 2026
- Positron Assistant, through Posit AI Pass: Claude Sonnet 5 for the first 80 replies, then Kimi K3 for the last 83
- From "Create a new R package called compliment" to moods, farewells, profanity, a README and a pkgdown index
- The conversation ends on 2 October with: *"Your Posit AI Pass credits have been depleted."*

::: {.notes}
The package started at the workshop as `compliment`.
Amelia chose the features and tested the output in the console herself.
The model behind Positron Assistant changed partway through workshop day; the export records both.
Work continued on 28 September and 2 October, and the conversation stops mid-task when the workshop credits ran out.
The first git commit is 28 September; the whole package arrived in one commit.
:::

## The `weirdness` dial took four tries {.smaller}

1. A `mode` argument: `"classic"` or `"unhinged"`
2. A number from 0 to 1, but one coin flip per compliment: 0 and 0.5 gave the *same* compliment that day
3. A coin flip per word ("Option A")
4. Three tiers, classic, quirky and bizarre, blended by weight ("Option B")

About a dozen prompts were the assistant's own suggested next step, sent back word for word.
Pair programming, where the pair also drafts your half.

::: {.notes}
Design 2 replaced `mode` when the request was to add a parameter, and Amelia found out when an old call failed.
She also noticed that weirdness 0 and 0.5 gave identical output, and asked why: one random draw decided everything.
After that, the next redesign came to her as options first, and she chose: "start with a but document a plan to implement b later."
The suggested-next-step pattern is the tool working as designed: it offers the next step and you can click it.
:::

## Stage 2: Claude Code {.smaller}

- 9 October: renamed `compliment` to **pleasantry** (it makes farewells too, and a pleasantry is also a jest), moved to the repository root
- 13 October: pkgdown site built and deployed by GitHub Actions
- From 23 October: mostly one long Claude Code conversation: reviews, fixes, expanded word lists, word groups
- Four pull requests, each merged on Amelia's yes

Models: commits from 9 to 13 October name Claude Opus 5; the later conversation ran on Claude Opus 5.5.

::: {.notes}
The October rename and move came from a Claude Code session whose commits carry a Claude Opus 5 trailer.
That session could not change repository settings, so it said so and left the rename and GitHub Pages to Amelia.
From late October most of the work ran in one long Claude Code conversation, resumed in November; the 2 November pull request came from a separate cloud session.
The last pull request merged on 6 November, after Amelia wrote: "If it's ready to merge do it."
It was, and the agent did.
:::

## Who did what {.smaller}

**Amelia decided**: what to build, which fixes, the word-group design, AI attribution in commits, every merge, and every push from her machine.

**The agents did**: the code, tests and docs; subagents for the word lists and some of the reviews, the word-list one working from a written task contract.

**Five review rounds** from 23 October to 4 November, and the main session checked the subagents' work before relying on it.

::: {.notes}
Pushing and merging are not delegated in this repository: the project profile says they wait for Amelia's yes.
When an approval to push came before a review had finished, the agent stopped and showed her the new findings first.
A task contract here is a short brief: scope, what not to touch, and how we will know it is right.
:::

## How it is checked

- 36 tests in 4 files (testthat edition 3), seeds scoped with `withr`
- `R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (new submission)
- From 31 October, each bug fix came with a test, shown able to fail by breaking the code on purpose
- pkgdown site rebuilt by GitHub Actions on every push to `main`

::: {.notes}
The R CMD check result is the one reported in the last fix commit, 4 November.
"Shown able to fail": the agent broke the code in a throwaway copy and confirmed the new test caught it.
The only GitHub Actions workflow builds the documentation site; there is no CI check workflow.
:::

## What went wrong, and what changed {.smaller}

- `.Rbuildignore` comments were live regex: it has no comment syntax. Removed.
- *"Few people have a energy as creative as yours."* Now `{a}` picks the article.
- *"remarkably remarkable"*, *"glorious glory"*. Now every word of four letters or more is compared on its first four.
- A profane suffix repeated a word the sentence already had. Now checked after profanity is added.
- A redraw loop with no exit. Now 100 tries, then an error.
- 15 MB of transcripts in a 12 KB package. Moved to their own branch.

::: {.notes}
Most of these were found by review rounds, not by users.
The article bug was checked over 40,000 strings once fixed, and the review of that fix found "a uninspired" and "a onerous".
The repeated-word suffix showed up 30 times in 200 runs on the old code; the exact phrase is in the appendix, behind the warning.
The transcripts move matters because installing from GitHub downloads the default branch.
:::

## What you could reuse

- Ask for options before a redesign, not after
- Test the output yourself: the 0 versus 0.5 tie was found in the console
- Review in rounds, and have a fresh agent do one
- Keep outward steps (push, merge) as your own yes
- Keep the transcript: this talk was written from it

::: {.notes}
Each of these is something that happened in this project.
The transcripts are public on the repository's dev-transcripts branch, so the dead ends are readable next to the result.
:::

## AI disclosure {.smaller}

- **Positron Assistant** (Claude Sonnet 5, then Kimi K3, via Posit AI Pass) wrote the package code at the workshop, steered and tested by Amelia.
- **Claude Code** (Claude Opus 5, then Claude Opus 5.5) did the rename, the move, the review rounds, the fixes and the expanded word lists; Amelia chose the fixes and approved every merge.
- **This deck** was built by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) from research notes on the git history and both transcripts; every claim is traced to its source in `talk/claims.md`, for a fresh reviewer agent and Amelia to check.

::: {.notes}
The model names come from the transcripts and the commit trailers, not from memory.
The word lists were chosen by an agent, and the repository's TODO says no person has read them.
:::

# Appendix {.center}

## Content warning {.center}

The next slides show the `"strong"` profanity level.
It is real swearing.

## `profanity = "strong"`

```{r}
set.seed(3)
compliment(mood = "dramatic", profanity = "strong")
set.seed(8)
compliment(mood = "dramatic", profanity = "strong")
```

## The repeated-word bug, uncensored

In the dramatic mood, a compliment using "magnificent" could end with the suffix "you magnificent bastard".
On the old code the test sentence did it 30 times in 200 runs (commit `496768e`).
The fix leaves out any profanity phrase that shares a word with the sentence.

## The stem check

`R/banks.R` at `f2d62c1`:

```r
word_stems <- function(text) {
  words <- unlist(strsplit(tolower(gsub("\\{[^}]*\\}", " ", text)), "[^a-z]+"))
  unique(substr(words[nchar(words) >= 4], 1, 4))
}

stems_clash <- function(x, y) {
  length(intersect(word_stems(x), word_stems(y))) > 0
}
```
